Subject: Scheduling Challenge for a Multi-Mode, Resource-Constrained Project

Overview
We are preparing the baseline plan for a project that contains multiple interdependent activities competing for limited renewable resources. Each activity can be carried out in one of several execution modes, each mode representing a different speed/cost/resource profile. Our task is to coordinate mode selections and start times so that all activities meet their dependency relationships and timing requirements, while staying within the fixed project budget and minimizing the total time to complete the project.

Execution Modes and Trade-offs
Every activity must be executed in exactly one mode. Faster modes shorten task duration but typically require more resources and incur higher costs. Slower modes reduce cost and resource demand but extend the schedule. The mode we choose for each activity will therefore affect both the project’s timeline and its total spending.

Dependencies and Timing Requirements
The activities are linked by precedence relationships that define the order of work. Some links require a minimum delay between the finish of a predecessor and the start of its successor, ensuring necessary handoffs or waiting periods. A subset of links also enforce a maximum delay: the successor must start within a limited time window after the predecessor completes to maintain continuity and avoid stale work. In addition, certain activities cannot start before a specified date (release dates), and a number of activities must finish by a hard deadline.

Resource Framework and Safety Rule
The project relies on multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity. Resources are released as soon as an activity finishes, and activities cannot be preempted; once started, they run to completion in their chosen mode.

To ensure we never risk overloading any resource, we apply a conservative, pairwise safety rule for activities that are not connected by precedence: if there exists at least one combination of their modes and at least one resource for which the combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities must not overlap in time. In such cases, we will sequence them—one must finish before the other starts—and the schedule will determine which one goes first. This pairwise non-overlap rule is the only resource constraint we enforce; there is no additional “at all times” capacity check beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions.

Budget and Cost Control
The total cost of the modes we select across all activities must not exceed the fixed budget. This creates a balancing act between choosing faster, more expensive modes to compress the timeline and selecting slower, more economical modes to preserve funds.

Scheduling Challenge
The scheduling problem is to:
- Select exactly one mode for each activity.
- Determine start times that respect all precedence links, including both minimum and maximum delay requirements.
- Enforce release dates (earliest start times) and hard deadlines (required completion times).
- Apply the pairwise resource safety rule, adding sequencing between independent activities whenever their potential mode combinations could exceed resource capacity.
- Keep the total mode costs within the project budget.
- Minimize the overall project duration (makespan) while satisfying all the above.

Implications for Planning
The combination of execution-mode choices, conservative resource conflict avoidance, and timing constraints makes this a tightly coupled planning exercise. The team must identify where faster modes provide the greatest schedule benefit within the budget and where sequencing choices can alleviate resource contention without violating release dates, maximum delay requirements, or deadlines. The data necessary to support this analysis is summarized in the annex.
